subject: Clarifying default storage: streamed fragments, KV cache snapshots, and final answers
messages:
From: Daniel Cho <daniel.cho@navitashealth.com>
To: sergio_alvarez@redwood.com
Cc: compliance@navitashealth.com
Date: 2026-06-12T09:14:00-07:00
Subject: Question: streamed endpoints and what you keep by default

Hi Sergio,

Quick question from our privacy/compliance review — we use Redwood's streaming endpoints to get partial transcripts into our EHR ingestion pipeline. Our procurement needs a clear statement about what Redwood *stores by default* for streaming requests:

- Are in-flight streamed token fragments (partial transcripts sent progressively to the client) persisted to logs or object storage by default?
- Do KV cache snapshots, used to warm sessions, ever get written to durable storage or audit logs?
- What counts as the canonical "final output" vs a derivative or telemetry artifact?

We also need to understand deletion proof: if Navitas requests erasure for a specific patient session, what evidence can Redwood provide that both the request and any intermediate fragments were removed?

Attached is the short questionnaire our legal team sent over. We can schedule a quick call if that's easier.

Thanks,
Daniel
Director, Integration Platforms
Navitas Health

Attachment: navitas_retention_questionnaire.pdf
From: sergio_alvarez@redwood.com
To: Daniel Cho <daniel.cho@navitashealth.com>
Cc: neha_kapoor@redwood.com, karthik_iyer@redwood.com
Date: 2026-06-12T09:45:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Question: streamed endpoints and what you keep by default

Hi Daniel — thanks for the clear list. Short answers up front, then a slightly longer explanation and next steps below.

Short answers:
- Streamed token fragments: NOT retained by default. Streaming buffer fragments are kept in-memory while a session is active but are not written to durable logs unless a customer enables session logging or the diagnostics/debug flag.
- KV cache snapshots: Ephemeral only. We do not persist KV cache snapshots to long-term object storage by default; they are kept in volatile memory on the serving nodes and discarded when the session ends or the worker is recycled.
- Canonical final outputs: The canonicalized final output (the completed response returned by the API) is what we record as the request/response artifact by default, along with minimal metadata (request id, timestamps, model version, route).

Longer explanation / nuance:
- Streaming vs final output: For the hosted API, streaming fragments are treated as transient network buffers unless you opt into session recording (route-level flag: session_recording = true). When session_recording is on we persist the full stream with a retention TTL (default 45 days unless changed).
- Telemetry: We capture telemetry (latency, token counts, error traces) by default for platform health. Those records do not include full token text unless diagnostics are enabled.
- Deletion / proof: When a customer requests erasure, we run the purge across three layers: (1) index/catalog entry (so the record is no longer discoverable), (2) object store blobs (if any were created for that session), and (3) backup/tombstone indices (where applicable). We provide a signed confirmation with the purge job id and log snippet showing the purge timestamps. For streamed fragments that were never persisted there is no object to delete; we document that in the erasure evidence.

Question for you: do you currently have session_recording enabled on the routes used for EHR ingestion? If not, the default behavior should satisfy most of the "no intermediate text stored" requirements. If you need absolute assurance, we can provide a per-route auto-prune policy (0-day retention) plus an optional pre-ingest hook that drops/obfuscates PII before it reaches the streaming client.

Next steps I suggest:
1) If you can send the list of endpoint routes and whether session_recording is enabled, we will generate a one-page statement for procurement.
2) Neha (cc'd) will prepare a sample proof-of-deletion packet (signed, includes purge job id + time) for one recent sample session.
3) If required, we can propose a configuration (route-level retention tag + auto-prune=0) and schedule a 30-minute walkthrough.

Hope this helps — happy to jump on a call.

— Sergio
Principal Sales Engineer, Redwood Inference
From: Daniel Cho <daniel.cho@navitashealth.com>
To: sergio_alvarez@redwood.com
Cc: compliance@navitashealth.com
Date: 2026-06-12T11:03:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Question: streamed endpoints and what you keep by default

Thanks, Sergio — this is helpful. A couple clarifications from our side: 

> On Fri, Jun 12, 2026 at 9:45 AM Sergio Alvarez <sergio_alvarez@redwood.com> wrote:
> > Short answers:
> > - Streamed token fragments: NOT retained by default.

We are not using session_recording. Our worry is twofold: 1) even if fragments are in-memory, can a debug incident or autoscaling snapshot cause them to be temporarily written to disk or a crash dump? 2) our legal team wants a statement that any in-memory-only artifacts cannot be retrieved after the session ends (i.e., no crash dumps, no ephemeral swap).

Also: we use three routes: /v1/stream/transcribe-ehr, /v1/stream/annotate, /v1/complete/summary. Can you confirm whether auto-prune per-route tags are available, and whether we can set auto-prune=0 for /v1/stream/transcribe-ehr? Finally, we need a short, itemized procurement-ready line: one paragraph that says exactly what Redwood retains by default for streaming and KV cache.

If it helps, we need the procurement paragraph + the sample proof-of-deletion packet by next Tuesday (2026-06-16).

Daniel

Attachments: none
From: neha_kapoor@redwood.com
To: Daniel Cho <daniel.cho@navitashealth.com>
Cc: sergio_alvarez@redwood.com, karthik_iyer@redwood.com
Date: 2026-06-13T15:42:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Question: streamed endpoints and what you keep by default

Hi Daniel — looping back with the concrete artifacts we promised.

1) Procurement paragraph (copy/paste for contract team):
"By default, Redwood Inference persists the canonical completed response produced by our API (final output), together with minimal request metadata (request id, timestamp, model version, and route). In-flight streamed token fragments and KV cache snapshots are not written to durable logs or object storage by default. Streaming buffers are kept in volatile memory for the duration of the session only and are not recoverable after session termination unless a customer enables session_recording or diagnostics; in such cases, persisted session recordings are subject to the configured retention TTL. Redwood does not intentionally include streamed fragments or KV cache contents in crash dumps, and customers may request evidence of purge for persisted artifacts via a signed purge job record."

2) Sample proof-of-deletion packet (attached): redwood-erase-runbook-v1.md — this is a short runbook showing the steps our purge job takes, example log snippets, and the format of the signed confirmation we provide. Note: for sessions that never persisted fragments, the packet documents the check we perform (no object found) and the signed statement we return.

3) Per-route auto-prune: yes — we support a per-route retention tag. We can set auto-prune=0 for /v1/stream/transcribe-ehr; I have asked engineering to schedule the config change and will confirm when it's applied.

4) Crash-dump/swap question: by design, we avoid writing user token content to disk. Our standard crash-dump process scrubs buffers that match request id patterns; engineering has instrumented the core runtime to avoid dumping token payloads. If you require a formal attestation, we can provide the crash-dump scrub policy and a short note from our infra team.

Next steps:
- I will upload the runbook and a signed sample purge packet to the Drive link (https://drive.redwood.com/navitas/retention-qna) and share with your procurement.
- Sergio will coordinate the per-route auto-prune change and confirm once live.

If you'd like to accept this as the formal procurement language, confirm and we'll push it into the DPA addendum.

Best,
Neha Kapoor
Security & Compliance, Redwood Inference

Attachments: redwood-erase-runbook-v1.md
